notes.meaning: Zophar is the third of Job's friends to speak. The older commentators see him as the harshest of the three. Eliphaz began gently and Bildad was rougher, but Zophar attacks Job without mercy.

Zophar calls Job a 'man of lips,' someone who is all talk. He says Job's words are empty boasting and that Job mocks without anyone shaming him. Matthew Henry says this is unfair. Job's speeches were full of good sense, and any heat in them deserved kindness, not insults.

Zophar claims Job said, 'My teaching is right and I am pure before God.' But Job never claimed to be sinless. He had even said, 'I have sinned.' He only insisted that he was not a hypocrite, someone who pretends to be good while hiding sin.

Zophar wishes God would speak up and take his side against Job. Matthew Henry notes the irony. When God finally did speak at the end of the book, He spoke for Job and against the three friends. We are often too quick to assume God agrees with us in our arguments.

Zophar says God's wisdom has hidden depths, far greater than anything we can see. 'Two sides' (literally 'double') means it is much bigger than what has been shown to us. Then he tells Job that God is punishing him less than his sin deserves. Another way to read it is that God is overlooking much of Job's guilt. Matthew Henry says it is true that our troubles are always less than our sins deserve. But Zophar wrongly uses this truth against Job.

Here Zophar says something true and beautiful about God. No one can search out God completely. His greatness is higher than the sky, deeper than Sheol (the world of the dead), longer than the earth and wider than the sea. Matthew Henry says we can truly know God, but we can never fully understand Him. So we should speak of Him humbly.

The picture is of a courtroom. God may arrest someone, call a court together and pass sentence, and no one can stop Him or turn Him back. Adam Clarke thinks Zophar may be hinting at Job's own losses: his children taken, his body struck and his goods carried off.
We know little of God, but God knows us completely. He sees through people who hide their emptiness behind a show of goodness. He notices sin even when it is done in secret, and He will deal with it.

Zophar uses a saying. An empty-headed man will become wise about as soon as a wild donkey is born a human. Matthew Henry takes it to mean that people are proud and want to seem wise, yet by nature they are stubborn and hard to teach. Keil & Delitzsch see it as a jab at Job, though it really fits Zophar himself.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Hebrew here is hard, and translators differ. Some scholars read the verse more hopefully: through God's discipline even an empty man can gain understanding.

notes.meaning: Zophar calls Job to repent, which means to turn from sin back to God. Job should set his heart toward God, lift his hands in humble prayer, put away any sin he is holding onto, and keep wrongdoing out of his home. It is good advice in itself. But Zophar wrongly assumes Job must be hiding some sin, or else he would not be suffering.

If Job turns back to God, he will lift up his face without shame and stand firm without fear. These words answer Job's own complaint that he could not lift up his head (10:15). Matthew Henry adds a Christian application. When we are washed by Christ's blood, we may come boldly to God with a clear conscience (Hebrews 10:22).
Job's misery would fade from memory like water that has flowed past. The picture is a flash flood. It does great damage for a while, then quickly drains away and is gone.
Job's life would shine brighter than noon. Even if darkness came, it would only be like early morning, which grows lighter and lighter. In Scripture, light often stands for blessing and good times.

Job would feel safe because he would have real hope. He would look over his home, find all well, and sleep in peace with no one to frighten him. Many people would come seeking his friendship. Matthew Henry says hope in God is an anchor for the soul. Still, Zophar wrongly thinks good times always come back in this life to those who do right.

Zophar ends with a warning. People who refuse to turn from sin will look for help in vain and find no way of escape. Their hope will slip away like a dying man's last breath. Adam Clarke sums up the speech this way: Zophar's ideas were mostly good, but he applied them wrongly to Job.
